Learning Objectives
Determine when to refer a patient to orthopaedic oncology.
Summarize important features of prebiopsy planning.
Review the advantages and disadvantages of various biopsy techniques.
Describe the basic principles of biopsy.
Role of Biopsy
Biopsy establishes a definitive diagnosis.
Diagnosis guides management.
The goal is to perform a safe procedure that results in an accurate diagnosis


Role of Biopsy
A patient encounter begins with a clinical history and physical examination followed by
imaging studies and possibly a laboratory workup. If findings suggest an active or
aggressive process, biopsy is indicated. The biopsy establishes a diagnosis, which helps
determine the treatment plan. The intent of biopsy is to make a timely, accurate
diagnosis with the least morbidity and least contamination while maintaining all possible
treatment options.
Biopsy Principles
Biopsy should be planned by a surgeon capable of definitive management.
The approach should be along an incision necessary to perform oncologic resection.
Measures should be taken to minimize contamination and bleeding.
Frozen section can be performed to confirm the presence of lesional tissue.
The specimen should be sent for culture and surgical pathology

Biopsy Principles
The basic tenant of biopsy is to assume that a lesion is a localized malignancy with
curative potential until proven otherwise. Biopsy should be performed or directed by a
surgeon capable of definitive management. The biopsy approach should be in-line with
an incision that would be used for oncologic resection because the biopsy track will
potentially be contaminated by tumor and should be amenable to en bloc resection with
the tumor specimen. If possible, a tourniquet should be used with gravity
exsanguination to minimize bleeding during the procedure because bleeding may lead
to tumor seeding. The surgeon should come straight down to the tumor within one
anatomic compartment, away from critical structures such as nerves, vessels, tendons,
and joints. No-to-minimal flap elevation should occur. If possible, a frozen section should
be sent to confirm the presence of lesional tissue and confirm that the biopsy specimen
can be used to make a diagnosis. Hemostasis is imperative, and the use of hemostatic
agents, electrocautery, multilayer closure, and local compression should be considered.

In appropriate circumstances, a drain can be placed via an outside-in technique and kept
in-line and close to the surgical incision (Figure 1). Irrigation of the biopsy track typically
is avoided. If necessary, irrigation should be gentle and quick. Suture bites are
conservative and not too deep. All actions have the intent of minimizing potential tumor
spread along the biopsy access point. Neoplastic processes and infection may have
similar presentations and imaging appearances. Cultures should be sent during any
biopsy procedure.
Figure 1
Intraoperative photographs of a right shoulder show a transverse incision used for biopsy (A) and
a drain site exiting away from the biopsy incision (B). Both are incisional biopsies that were
performed at an outside institution. (Courtesy of Robert Steffner, MD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Pitfalls
A poorly performed biopsy affects diagnosis and future treatment options.
SEND FEEDBACK


Pitfalls
A poor biopsy frequently leads to insufficient sample and no diagnosis. Consequences
are additional procedures and a delay in the initiation of management. Sampling error
may lead to an inappropriate diagnosis, which leads to the incorrect treatment plan.
Nonadherence to biopsy principles and inappropriate biopsy planning lead to a broad
and contaminated biopsy track that may prevent limb salvage or require more morbid
soft-tissue coverage procedures, such as free tissue transfer.
Planning
General Considerations
Specific areas of a tumor may provide better diagnostic yield.
The biopsy tract should be resectable with the lowest possible morbidity.
Local anesthetic often is appropriate and administered before biopsy.

General Considerations
In addition to having a biopsy approach in-line with a possible future resection incision,
the biopsy site should target a location within the tumor at which tissue is viable and
representative of the concern for malignancy. The approach ignores traditional
intermuscular and internervous planes and aims to take a direct path to tumor through
tissue that can be resected with minimal functional morbidity. The manner in which the
biopsy approach will be documented or marked for future identification also should be
considered. Local anesthetic generally is adequate; however, it should be administered
before tumor sampling. Use of a local anesthetic is best avoided in patients with a
subcutaneous tumor and patients with a tumor close to the skin surface. Post-procedure
management also influences biopsy outcome. Applying a compressive wrap for a few
hours after a procedure, temporary joint immobilization, and instructions for rest and
elevation may help to minimize contamination.

Imaging Studies
MRI is critical for tumor evaluation and biopsy planning.
Positron emission tomography may guide the best area of tumor to sample.

Imaging Studies
MRI following protocols for bone and soft-tissue masses are vital in determining the
need for biopsy. MRI alone can be diagnostic for lipoma, nerve sheath tumors, and
vascular malformations (Figures 2 and 3). If imaging studies are nonspecific and cannot
rule out malignancy, MRI helps define the extent of tumor involvement; conveys a sense
of tumor homogeneity or heterogeneity; and, via the administration of contrast,
distinguishes areas of viable tumor tissue from those of necrosis. In addition, T1-
weighted MRIs show the location of surrounding critical structures and the proximity of
joint involvement (Figure 4). Ultrasonography can be performed to determine how well
an anatomic location and the mass itself can be visualized, which helps determine the
utility of image-guided needle biopsy. Positron emission tomography/CT can show
differential metabolic activity within an anatomic area or within a mass itself. This may
aid in determining the need for biopsy in evaluating for a possible local recurrence or in
localizing the best area to sample tissue within a mass.
Figure 2
Axial MRIs of a right hip with a subcutaneous mass show a high signal intensity on an T1-
weighted view (A); homogenous fat suppression on a T2-weighted fat-suppressed view
(B); and no enhancement on a T1-weighted, fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced view (C).
These findings are diagnostic for a lipoma. (Courtesy of Robert Steffner, MD, Palo Alto,
CA.)

Future Management
Surgeons must think about the manner in which a biopsy may affect future surgical
managemen.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM


Future Management
Surgeons must think a few steps ahead. Irrespective of biopsy technique, the approach
should consider the surgical approach necessary for definitive, potentially curative,
resection surgery. In most patients, a longitudinal incision should be used. Transverse
incisions are used in certain anatomic locations, such as the buttocks, anterior
pelvis/inguinal region, shoulder girdle/clavicle, and iliac crest. This reinforces the need
for biopsy to be performed or directed by an individual who will be involved in
performing definitive resection surgery.
Tests
Differential diagnosis guides the types of tests ordered at biopsy.
Some tests only can be performed on fresh-frozen tissue.

Tests
Frozen section analysis can be performed to confirm that diagnostic tissue is obtained
during a biopsy procedure. Biopsy samples should be sent for culture and surgical
pathology. Cultures often are sent for aerobic, anaerobic, acid-fast bacillus, and fungal
testing. Clinical features and imaging studies determine the extent of microbiology
evaluation. Specimens for surgical pathology are sent in formalin and normal saline
(Figure 5). Formalin immediately fixes tissue to maintain appearance and architecture.
Immunohistochemical and fluorescence in situ hybridization studies can be performed
with fixed specimens. Tissue in normal saline is fresh and stored in a freezer. This tissue
can be used for cytogenetics or flow cytometry. If a specimen is being saved for tissue
banking or research purposes, surgeons should coordinate with research personnel
before biopsy.

Figure 5
Photograph shows biopsy specimens in formalin for fixed tissue analysis (left); sterile,
normal saline for fresh analysis (middle); and a culture tube (right). The sterile, normal
saline is placed in a freezer for tissue preservation. This allows for complete testing of
the biopsied lesion. (Courtesy of Robert Steffner, MD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Techniques
Fine-Needle Aspiration
Aspiration technique that attains individual tumor cells
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) requires cytologic evaluation.
Tissue architecture cannot be assessed.
Used to evaluate local recurrence and distinguish benign tumors from malignant tumors.

Fine-Needle Aspiration
A small needle and serial aspirations are used in FNA to obtain single cells. Cytologic
interpretation is required for diagnosis. Because no tissue architecture is present and
samples are limited, this technique is primarily used for assessing local recurrence or
distinguishing benign samples from malignant samples. Evidence shows that FNA can be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | Musculoskeletal Tumor Biopsy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004039
9/17

accurate in diagnosing high-grade sarcoma, bone sarcomas, and pediatric sarcomas.1,2
FNA requires an experienced cytopathologist.
Core Biopsy
Technique attains solid tube of tissue
Allows for evaluation of tissue architecture.
Accurate in establishing malignancy and tumor grade
Preferred technique in most circumstances

Core Biopsy
Core biopsy involves the use of a large-gauge needle with a hollow bore to sharply
remove a core of tissue (Figure 6). The biopsy is performed percutaneously, and the
needle can be redirected through the same starting site to obtain samples from multiple
areas within a tumor. Sample volume is variable, which may be a limitation. Tissue
architecture is maintained, which facilitates accurate diagnosis. Core biopsy is very
accurate for establishing malignancy and tumor grade.3 Immediate cytologic evaluation
at the time of biopsy to verify the presence of lesional tissue improves diagnostic
yield.4,5 Studies show that the correct histologic diagnosis can be achieved in 84% to 87%
of patients.6,7 In general, this technique is associated with the lowest morbidity and can
be performed in the office setting via palpation or ultrasonographic guidance. Given
these advantages, core biopsy generally is considered the primary technique for biopsy
of trunk and extremity soft-tissue and bone lesions. Disadvantages of core biopsy are
potential sampling error and insufficient sample to make a diagnosis.

Figure 6
Photograph shows the needle tip of a 14-gauge core biopsy instrument and core biopsy
system (inset). The chamber extends 2 cm and obtains a solid core of tissue for analysis.
This preserves architecture, which aids in determining the histologic diagnosis.
(Reproduced with permission from IZI Medical, Baltimore, MD.)
Open/Incisional Biopsy
Sharply excising a portion of the tumor
Generally reserved for specific scenarios
Performed under general anesthesia
Higher risk of contamination

Open/Incisional Biopsy
An open biopsy is a procedure most commonly performed in the operating room under
general or regional anesthesia. A small incision is made, and tissue is sharply incised
from the lesion of interest. Frozen section analysis generally is performed to confirm the
presence of lesional tissue. Because of increased morbidity and cost, this technique is
most often used after nondiagnostic core biopsy. Additional indications include

9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | Musculoskeletal Tumor Biopsy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004039
11/17

suspected lymphoma in which additional tumor tissue is necessary for subtyping, bone
lesion without extraosseous soft-tissue extension, and high likelihood of complete tumor
resection after confirmatory frozen section analysis. This technique is associated with a
greater risk of biopsy track contamination;8 therefore, it should be performed by the
surgeon providing definitive treatment.
Excisional Biopsy
Complete mass removal at the time of biopsy
Commonly used for subcutaneous and small (<3 cm) masses
Can be used in patients with high diagnostic suspicion and for specific anatomic sites

Excisional Biopsy
An excisional biopsy involves removal of the entire mass before diagnosis. This approach
generally is reserved for small (≤3 cm) and subcutaneous masses, lesions that are
confirmed or strongly suggestive of benign behavior based on imaging studies and
patient history, and small masses in the hands and feet. Small and subcutaneous masses
most often are benign or non-neoplastic; they are malignant in approximately 7% of
patients.9 Additional considerations for complete resection without biopsy are cartilage
lesions with progressive growth observed on serial imaging studies; lesions with imaging
features classic for parosteal osteosarcoma or giant cell tumor of bone; and deep and
small masses, especially in extracompartmental spaces, such as the antecubital fossa,
popliteal fossa, and axilla. The surgeon must consider pretest probability, surgical
morbidity, and morbidity of re-excision in deciding to perform an excisional biopsy as a
marginal excision or as a wide resection.
Image-guided Biopsy
CT and ultrasonographic guided biopsies improve the accuracy of tissue sampling.
Surgeons must communicate with radiologists if they are asked to perform the biopsy.
Image guidance may be helpful in patients in whom initial biopsy is not diagnostic.
SEND FEEDBACK


Image-guided Biopsy
Core biopsy and FNA often are performed under image guidance with the use of
ultrasonography or CT to improve the accuracy of tissue sampling. These imaging
modalities are necessary for deep masses that are not palpable. In addition, image
guidance prevents past pointing, or accidental extension of the needle tip through and
beyond a tumor and into surrounding normal tissue. Although not studied, this
theoretically contaminates surrounding tissue and creates an increased risk for local
recurrence. Radiologists often perform biopsies under image guidance, and good
communication with the surgeon is mandatory. Additional considerations for image
guidance are masses with a myxoid appearance, heterogeneity observed on imaging
studies, and extensive central necrosis observed on contrast-enhanced MRIs (Figure 7).
If core biopsy is repeated under image guidance after an initial nondiagnostic biopsy, a
diagnosis is achieved in 48% of patients.10
Figure 7
Axial (A) and coronal (B) T1-weighted, fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced MRIs of a right
medial thigh show a soft-tissue sarcoma with central necrosis. (Courtesy of Robert
Steffner, MD, Palo Alto, CA.)
Considerations
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004039
13/17

Diagnosis requires concordance between the patient history, imaging studies, and tissue
histology.
No increase in local recurrence has been observed after core needle biopsy with or without en
bloc resection of the biopsy tract.
Surgeons must document the location of the biopsy approach for future reference.
Specific soft-tissue sarcoma histologies are associated with a risk of lymph node involvement,
and sentinel lymph node biopsy should be considered.

Considerations
Any biopsy specimen should be evaluated in terms of its histologic appearance, patient
history and physical examination, and imaging appearance in determining a diagnosis.
Rare diagnoses benefit from presentations at specialty tumor boards and, occasionally,
from second opinions by outside pathologists. If a biopsy is nondiagnostic, surgeons
should pursue a biopsy approach that will result in more tissue in high-yield locations of
the lesion. Surgeons also should consider expanding the list of potential diagnoses.
Biopsy should be performed or guided by the surgeon providing definitive treatment.
Pre-referral procedures lead to more complications.11 In addition, the type of biopsy
selected is an important detail in the patient’s overall oncologic care. Core biopsy is the
preferred option for biopsy because it minimizes contamination. Studies have found no
increase in tumor local recurrence with and without en bloc resection of biopsy track
from core biopsies.12 This includes patients who did not receive radiation.13 Open
biopsy leads to histologic seeding of the biopsy track in 32% of the patients, which is
associated with an increased risk of local recurrence.8 It also is important that the
location of a biopsy track is documented to allow for en bloc resection at the time of
definitive surgery. Identification of the location of core biopsy tracks weeks after the
biopsy procedure may be a challenge, if not impossible.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is a technique used to identify lymph nodes that receive
lymphatic fluid drainage from the area of tumor growth. Seventeen percent of patients
with soft-tissue sarcoma have a positive sentinel lymph node biopsy, which is associated
with increased mortality.14 Clear cell sarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma,

angiosarcoma, and synovial sarcoma are sarcoma subtypes with documented spread to
regional lymph nodes. A sentinel lymph node biopsy should be considered for these
diagnoses.
